Before you mix anything, you need to know why each product works, what every raw material in your store is, and how to set up a room where acids, alkalis and bleach can never meet by accident. This module builds that foundation for the six products you will make in Modules 2 and 3.

Every product in this course does one or more of three jobs: it **lifts dirt** (grease, oil, food, body soil), it **dissolves deposits** (limescale, rust stains, urine scale), or it **kills germs** on a surface. A production business that understands these three jobs makes fewer mistakes, sells the right product to each customer and writes honest directions on the label.
Soap bubbles
Foam is a sign that surfactant is present, but cleaning power comes from what happens at the surface of the dirt.
Surfactants: the molecules that do the lifting

Water alone cannot remove grease because oil and water do not mix. A **surfactant** (short for surface active agent) is a molecule with two ends. One end loves water. The other end loves oil. When you wash, the oil-loving ends push into the grease and the water-loving ends stay in the water. With rubbing, the grease breaks into tiny droplets that are surrounded by surfactant, so they float away in the rinse water instead of settling back.
Surfactants are grouped by the electric charge on the water-loving end. You will use three groups in this course:
**Anionic** (negative charge): LAS, made from sulphonic acid, and SLES (sold as "texapon"). Strong cleaners and good foamers. The base of laundry and dish products.
**Nonionic** (no charge): alcohol ethoxylates such as the AEO-9 grade. Good on oily soil, low foam, and they still work in acid products and next to disinfectants.
**Cationic** (positive charge): benzalkonium chloride (BKC), a quaternary ammonium compound used as a disinfectant. Weak cleaner, but it kills many germs.
Opposite charges cancel each other

Anionic and cationic surfactants attract each other and form a sticky, cloudy complex that does neither job well. Never add BKC to a dish liquid or laundry detergent made with LAS or SLES. You will see this with your own eyes in Lesson 3.3.
pH: choosing acid or alkaline

The **pH scale** runs from 0 to 14. Pure water is 7 (neutral). Below 7 is acid; above 7 is alkaline. Each step is ten times stronger than the one next to it, so pH 2 is ten times more acidic than pH 3. You will measure pH with paper strips (cheap, good enough to start) or a pen-type pH meter (more exact, needs calibration).

The four cleaning forces

Cleaning experts describe four forces that work together, often drawn as a circle: **chemistry** (the product), **action** (scrubbing, agitation, spraying), **temperature** (warm water melts grease faster) and **time** (how long the product stays on the dirt). If one force goes down, another must go up. A hotel laundry with hot water and a machine needs less chemistry than a woman washing by hand in cold borehole water.
Chemistry: the product
Action: scrubbing or agitation
Temperature: warm water
Time: contact before rinsing
Reduce one force and you must increase another to get the same clean result.

This matters for your labels. When you write "leave for 10 minutes before brushing" on a toilet cleaner, you are using time to do work that chemistry alone cannot do. When you advise soaking heavily soiled clothes, you are adding time. Good directions are part of the product.

**Hard water** is the other thing to know. Borehole and well water in many parts of Nigeria carry dissolved calcium and magnesium. These minerals react with anionic surfactants and waste some of their power, which is why laundry detergents contain a **builder** such as soda ash (sodium carbonate) to soften the water first.
Worked example: matching four complaints to four products

For example, Ngozi runs a small guest house in Owerri and asks you what she should buy. She lists four problems: greasy kitchen floors, yellow-brown rings in the toilets, cloudy bathroom mirrors, and towels that look grey.
Greasy kitchen floor: grease needs an alkaline surfactant cleaner, so you recommend the heavy-duty floor cleaner, diluted in warm water, with a scrubbing brush (action plus temperature).
Toilet rings: the yellow-brown ring is usually mineral scale with stains, which needs acid, so you recommend the acid toilet bowl cleaner left for 10 minutes before brushing (time).
Cloudy mirrors: a light film needs very little surfactant and a fast-drying solvent, so you recommend the glass cleaner, sprayed and wiped with a dry cloth.
Grey towels: soil building up in hard water, so you recommend the liquid laundry detergent with soda ash builder, a soak before washing, and the full dose on the label.
You warn her clearly: keep the toilet cleaner and any bleach apart, and never pour one after the other into the same toilet.

Ngozi leaves with three bottles and one keg that each fit a real problem, plus one safety rule. A matched recommendation brings repeat orders; a single "all-purpose" product that fails on the toilet ring does not.
The rule you will see in every module

Never mix bleach (sodium hypochlorite) with an acid product such as a toilet cleaner or vinegar: it releases chlorine gas. Never mix bleach with ammonia or ammonia-containing cleaners: it releases toxic chloramine gases. Both gases harm the eyes and lungs. This is why this course makes its acid toilet cleaner and its glass cleaner without bleach or ammonia.

Documents to ask for

Ask every supplier for two documents. The **safety data sheet (SDS)** is a standard 16-section sheet that lists the hazards, first aid, safe storage and what the chemical must not touch. The **certificate of analysis (COA)** states the measured strength of a particular lot, for example "active matter 96.2%" for LABSA. Big importers usually have both. If a seller has neither, buy a small amount, mark it "strength unknown" and do not base your formula on it.

On an SDS, read section 2 (hazards and pictograms), section 4 (first aid), section 7 (handling and storage) and section 10 (stability and reactivity, which lists the materials it must be kept away from). Copy the key lines into your own one-page summary and pin it in your store.
Checking a delivery
Check the container: closed, not leaking, not bulging, with a readable label showing the name and, ideally, the lot number.
Compare the label with your order and the COA: same material, same strength.
Look at the material: flakes should be dry and free-flowing, not wet lumps; SLES should be smooth paste, not watery.
Weigh it on your platform scale. Paying for 25 kg and receiving 23 kg is a 2 kg loss.
Write the date, supplier, lot number and weight in your raw-material book, then move it straight to its storage zone.
Worked example: checking a 25 kg SLES delivery
For example, Bisi in Ibadan orders 25 kg of SLES 70% for her dish liquid. The trader delivers a jerrycan with a hand-written label.
She asks for the COA. The trader shows a photo on WhatsApp of a COA stating active matter 70.1% for a lot number that matches the original drum label. She saves the photo.
She opens the jerrycan in her ventilated store. The paste is smooth and pale. A runny, watery paste would suggest dilution.
She weighs the full jerrycan: 26.4 kg. The empty jerrycan of the same type weighs 1.4 kg, so the net SLES is 26.4 minus 1.4, which is 25.0 kg.
She writes: date, supplier name, lot number, 25.0 kg, COA saved, "accepted".
Her formula needs 2.0 kg of SLES paste per 25 kg dish batch, so 25.0 kg is enough for 25.0 / 2.0 = 12 full batches, with 1.0 kg left over.
Bisi knows the strength, the quantity and the number of batches she can make before she reorders. If a batch ever behaves strangely, the lot number in her book leads her back to this delivery.

Keep isopropyl alcohol and fragrances in a fourth spot away from heat, sockets and any flame. Keep powders off the floor and sealed, because caustic soda absorbs moisture from the air and goes lumpy.

Worked example: setting up a 3 m by 4 m room
For example, Hauwa in Kaduna rents a single room behind her shop, 3 metres by 4 metres, with one door and one window, to make laundry detergent and dish liquid.
She puts the raw-material shelves on the wall farthest from the door, in four labelled zones, with acids at one end and bleach at the other.
Next to the shelves she places a sturdy table for the scale, so weighing happens beside the store.
She puts two 50-litre plastic mixing drums under the window, so fumes and dust move outside.
Near the door she sets a filling table and the finished-goods shelf, so bottles leave without passing the mixing drums.
Beside the mixing drums she keeps a 25-litre jerrycan of clean water with a tap, a clean eye-wash bottle, and a bucket of sand with a scoop for spills.
She pins the SDS summaries and the first-aid steps on the wall at eye level, and keeps children and customers out of the room.
Hauwa's room has a clear path from store to door, water within reach of every splash point, and no reason for concentrates to travel past finished products.
Order of addition: the rules that prevent boiling and splashing

**Caustic soda goes into water, slowly**, never water onto caustic soda. It heats up strongly as it dissolves. Use cold water in a heat-resistant plastic container, never aluminium, which caustic soda attacks.
**LABSA goes into water**, stirring, not water into a small pool of LABSA.
**Add the caustic solution to the diluted acid slowly**, in portions, and wait between portions. Neutralising produces heat.
**Never pour a bleach product into the same container, drain or toilet** as an acid product or any ammonia product.
Label every bucket with what is in it, even if it is only for an hour.
First aid you must know before you start

Eyes: rinse immediately with gently running clean water for at least 15 minutes, holding the eyelids open, then go to a clinic with the product label. Skin: remove contaminated clothing and rinse with plenty of running water for at least 15 minutes. Swallowed: do not make the person vomit; rinse the mouth, and get medical help at once, taking the container or label. Gas from mixed products: leave the room for fresh air at once, open doors and windows only if it is safe, and get medical help for coughing, burning or breathing difficulty. Do not use vinegar or other chemicals to "neutralise" a splash on skin or eyes.
Spills and waste

For a small liquid spill, stop the source, cover the spill with dry sand, scoop it into a labelled bucket and wash the area with plenty of water. For a caustic soda flake spill, sweep it up dry before adding any water. Rinse water from cleaning drums contains surfactant: use it to wash the room floor rather than pouring large amounts into a gutter. Never pour concentrates down a drain or onto soil.

Because you will store isopropyl alcohol and fragrances, keep a working fire extinguisher by the door, learn how to use it, and keep electrical sockets dry and away from the mixing drums. Lock the room when you leave it. A production room is a workplace, not a store room that children can wander into.

How much caustic soda?

One molecule of sulphonic acid reacts with one molecule of sodium hydroxide. Using their molecular weights (about 326 for the acid and 40 for sodium hydroxide), 1 kg of pure acid needs about 0.123 kg of caustic soda. For 96% LABSA, that becomes about 0.118 kg per kg. Commercial LABSA also contains a little free sulphuric acid, so you usually need slightly more. That is why you **calculate first, add about 90% of the calculation, then finish slowly by measuring pH**.
Worked example: the numbers for a 20 kg laundry batch
For example, Chiamaka in Onitsha supplies two laundries and wants a 20 kg batch of the formula above. Her LABSA COA says 96%.
LABSA: 20 kg x 8% = 1.60 kg.
Caustic soda by calculation: 1.60 x 0.118 = about 0.19 kg (189 g).
First addition, about 90%: 189 x 0.9 = about 170 g. She dissolves 190 g of flakes in 1.7 kg of cold water to make a roughly 10% solution, and adds it in portions.
SLES: 20 x 6% = 1.20 kg. Soda ash: 20 x 1% = 0.20 kg. CMC: 20 x 0.3% = 60 g.

Fixed ingredients so far: 1.60 + 0.19 + 1.20 + 0.20 + 0.06 = 3.25 kg. Water (including the water used for the caustic solution) is about 20 minus 3.25, which is 16.75 kg, minus any salt, fragrance and colour she adds.
Chiamaka's batch sheet lists every weight before she opens a single container. She will record the actual caustic used, because her finishing pH decides the final figure.
Production steps in order
Put on goggles, gloves, apron and long sleeves. Open the window.
Weigh about 12 kg of clean water into a 30 to 50 litre plastic drum.
Pour in the 1.60 kg of LABSA slowly while stirring with a long plastic or wooden paddle. The liquid turns cloudy brown.
In a separate labelled jug, dissolve the caustic soda flakes into cold water (flakes into water, never the reverse).
Add the caustic solution to the drum in four or five portions, stirring and waiting a few minutes between portions. The drum gets warm.
After about 90% of the calculated caustic, test the pH with a strip. Keep adding small amounts and testing until the pH is about 7 to 8. The liquid usually becomes clearer as it neutralises.
Dissolve the soda ash in a little warm water and stir it in. Adding soda ash only after neutralising avoids fizzing.
Sprinkle the CMC slowly onto the moving liquid, or premix it with a little SLES, to avoid lumps.
Add the SLES, pre-softened in some of the water, and stir gently to avoid excess foam.
Add colour, fragrance and preservative. Make up to 20 kg with water. Add salt solution in small steps only if you want it thicker.
Cover and rest overnight so foam and air bubbles rise out, then check pH (aim for about 9 to 10 after the soda ash) and fill.

If you overshoot and the pH reaches 9 or more before the soda ash, stop adding caustic. Stir in a very small amount of extra LABSA (for example 20 g at a time, poured into the drum, not the other way round), wait, and test again. Record exactly what you added. A product that is too alkaline is harsh on hands that wash clothes by hand.

CMC (sodium carboxymethyl cellulose) helps stop loosened dirt from settling back on the fabric during the wash. It is one reason white clothes stay white rather than slowly turning grey.

The neutralisation follows the same steps as Lesson 2.1: LABSA into water, caustic solution in portions, testing as you go. The difference is the end point. You stop at about pH 7 and add no soda ash. Then you add the SLES and thicken.
Thickening with salt, the controlled way

Salt thickens LAS and SLES blends up to a point. Past that point, the liquid becomes thin again and you cannot take the salt back out. So you never pour salt in by guesswork. Make a **25% salt solution** (250 g of salt dissolved in 750 g of water). Add it 100 g at a time, stir for two minutes, and check thickness each time by timing how long a fixed amount takes to flow, for example 100 ml through a funnel.

The brown-yellow ring in a toilet bowl is mostly mineral scale from hard water and urine, with stains trapped inside it. Surfactants alone cannot remove it. **Cleaning** removes dirt. **Disinfecting** kills germs on a surface. Disinfectants work much better on a surface that has already been cleaned, because dirt shields germs and uses up the active ingredient. That is why the directions for any disinfectant start with "clean first". In this lesson you make a disinfectant cleaner based on **benzalkonium chloride (BKC)**, a quaternary ammonium compound ("quat") widely used in hard-surface disinfectants.
A shield
A disinfectant protects only when used at the right strength, on a clean surface, for the right contact time.
Your supplier's sheet sets the numbers

BKC is usually sold as a **50% concentrate**. The level of BKC needed in your finished product, and the contact time needed to kill germs, depend on the grade of BKC and the germs you are targeting. Do not take these figures from social media. Use the in-use level and contact time stated on your supplier's technical data sheet for a hard-surface disinfectant, and write them into your batch sheet.

The concentrate can burn skin and cause serious eye damage. Wear splash goggles, gloves and an apron, weigh it in a ventilated room, and always add the concentrate to water. The diluted finished product is much milder but still needs the warning panel.

The jar test: why BKC stays away from anionics

Pour 100 ml of your finished disinfectant cleaner into a clear jar. Add a few drops of your dish liquid (which contains LAS and SLES) and stir. The liquid usually turns cloudy as the positively charged BKC and the negatively charged anionic surfactants grab each other. The BKC tied up in that cloud is no longer free to work on germs. This is why your disinfectant uses a nonionic surfactant only, why you clean the drum thoroughly between a dish batch and a disinfectant batch, and why your directions say to rinse soapy residues before disinfecting.

Honest claims
Do not print "kills 99.9% of germs" or name specific germs unless your product has been tested for that claim. That figure comes from laboratory testing, not from the formula.
Do not suggest the product protects people from any disease, or that it can be used on skin, in wounds or on food.
Do print the directions: clean the surface, apply undiluted, leave wet for the stated contact time, then wipe or rinse food-contact surfaces with clean water.
Do print the warning panel: keep out of reach of children, avoid eyes, do not mix with other products, first aid, and your batch number.

NAFDAC's MSME page lists the simple products that micro and small businesses can register through its simplified route, such as laundry detergents and soaps. Disinfectants are not on that list, so expect a fuller registration process for any product sold as a disinfectant, and speak to your NAFDAC state office before you sell one under that name.
Bleach is a separate product line

If you also repackage household bleach, never mix it with your disinfectant cleaner, toilet gel or any other product, and never make it in the same drum. Store it in opaque, closed HDPE containers away from sunlight and heat, which weaken it, and well away from your acid materials. Bleach must never be mixed with acids or with ammonia.

Explain contact time in plain words on the label and when you train a customer's cleaners: the surface must **stay wet** with the product for the full time stated. Spraying and wiping dry at once does not give the disinfectant time to work. For large areas, cleaners can apply it with a damp cloth or mop that leaves the surface visibly wet, then leave it before wiping or rinsing. A short demonstration with a timer on your phone makes this rule easy to remember.

Finally, keep each disinfectant batch record with the supplier's sheet and the COA for the BKC lot you used. If a hospital, school or hotel buyer asks how you know the strength is right, those three documents are your answer.

**Fill weight**: weigh ten filled bottles after taring the scale with an empty bottle and cap.

Stability: will it last on a shop shelf?

Before you launch a new formula, fill three bottles. Keep one at room temperature in the dark, one in a warm place such as a sunny window inside a closed room, and one in the coolest place you have. Check each week for a month: colour change, separation, haze, smell change, mould, bulging or a collapsed bottle. A product that separates in the warm bottle will separate in a hot market stall. Change the formula before selling, not after complaints.
Retained samples and complaints

Keep one small bottle from every batch, labelled with the batch number and date, for at least as long as the product's shelf life. When a customer complains, ask for the batch number from her label, take out your retained sample and the batch record, and compare. If your sample is fine, the problem may be storage or use, and you can show her the right directions. If your sample shows the same fault, you know which batch to recall and what went wrong.
Rework only what is safe to rework

Adding more salt, fragrance or water to correct flow or smell is normal rework. Never try to rescue a batch where you are unsure how much caustic soda, acid or BKC went in. Mark it "rejected", do not sell it, and ask your supplier or a chemist how to dispose of it safely.

Many small producers price by copying the bottle next to theirs in the market, then discover months later that they were working for free. The safe method is to cost every batch from your own batch sheet, then check that your price is competitive. Prices of LABSA, SLES and bottles change often in Nigeria, so update your costing sheet every time you restock.

The four parts of batch cost
**Raw materials**: every ingredient, by the weight in your batch sheet, at the price you actually paid.
**Packaging**: bottles, caps, labels and cartons for the number of units the batch fills.
**Labour**: your time and any helper's time, at a fair hourly rate. If you do not pay yourself, you cannot grow.
**Overheads**: a share of rent, electricity, transport, data and phone, PPE and testing materials.
Worked example: costing a 20 kg laundry batch in 1 litre bottles
For example, Chiamaka costs her 20 kg laundry batch from Lesson 2.1. The prices below are illustrative assumptions only, not current market prices; she uses the prices on her own receipts.

Raw materials (assumed prices): LABSA 1.6 kg at about ₦3,000/kg = ₦4,800; caustic soda 0.19 kg at about ₦2,000/kg = ₦380; SLES 1.2 kg at about ₦2,500/kg = ₦3,000; soda ash 0.2 kg at about ₦1,200/kg = ₦240; CMC 0.06 kg at about ₦4,000/kg = ₦240; fragrance 0.06 kg at about ₦15,000/kg = ₦900; colour and preservative ₦600; water ₦200. Total raw materials: ₦10,360.
Units: density 1.02 g/ml, so each 1 litre bottle takes 1,020 g. 20,000 / 1,020 = 19.6, so 19 full bottles, with 620 g kept as a retained sample and for testing.
Packaging: 19 bottles x (₦250 bottle and cap + ₦60 label) = 19 x ₦310 = ₦5,890.
Labour: 4 hours at ₦1,000 per hour = ₦4,000. Overheads share: ₦1,500.
Cost per bottle: 21,750 / 19 = about ₦1,145.
Each 1 litre bottle costs Chiamaka about ₦1,145 to make. Any price below that loses money, even if the bottle sells quickly.
From cost to price

Next, survey the market: note the price and size of three competing products in the shops and markets where you want to sell. Convert each to price per litre so you compare like with like. Then set two prices: a **wholesale price** for laundries, shops and resellers who buy in quantity, and a **retail price** for single bottles. The reseller needs room to make her own profit between the two.
Worked example: checking the margins
For example, Chiamaka sets a wholesale price of ₦1,700 and a retail price of ₦2,000 per litre, after checking that similar local brands sell at a comparable price per litre (her own survey).
Wholesale profit per bottle: 1,700 minus 1,145 = ₦555, which is 555 / 1,145 = about 48% on cost.
Wholesale profit per batch: (19 x 1,700) minus 21,750 = 32,300 minus 21,750 = ₦10,550.
Retail profit per batch: (19 x 2,000) minus 21,750 = 38,000 minus 21,750 = ₦16,250.
A reseller buying at ₦1,700 and selling at ₦2,000 earns ₦300 per bottle.
Chiamaka knows exactly what each channel earns her, and that labour and overheads are already paid inside the cost before profit is counted.

**Institutional buyers**: laundries, hotels, schools, hostels, churches and mosques, estates and offices. They buy in kegs on a regular schedule. Offer a sample, a demonstration and a written price list.
**Cleaning companies**: they need concentrates and refills that give a low cost per bucket. Your dilution ladder results are your sales tool.

Plan your week so that acid products, alkaline products and disinfectants are made on different days or in different drums, with drums washed and rinsed between products. This avoids contamination, such as LAS left in a drum turning your BKC cleaner cloudy, and it keeps the most hazardous steps away from busy filling days.

For example, Funke wins a supply contract and moves her dish liquid to 100 kg batches, still in 500 ml bottles at 515 g each.

Growing as a cooperative

A **cooperative**, as defined by the International Cooperative Alliance, is an autonomous association of people united voluntarily to meet their common economic, social and cultural needs through a jointly owned and democratically controlled enterprise. Its seven principles are: voluntary and open membership; democratic member control (one member, one vote in a primary cooperative); member economic participation; autonomy and independence; education, training and information; cooperation among cooperatives; and concern for community.
Worked example: bulk buying LABSA together

For example, five women in a Lagos market group each use about 8 kg of LABSA a month. A supplier offers a lower price for larger orders: suppose about ₦2,700 per kg for 40 kg instead of about ₦3,000 per kg for small amounts (illustrative figures only).
Combined monthly need: 5 x 8 = 40 kg.
Saving per kg: 3,000 minus 2,700 = ₦300.
Total monthly saving: 40 x 300 = ₦12,000, which is ₦2,400 per member.
They agree in writing who receives the delivery, how it is weighed out into labelled containers, and that each member pays her share before the order is placed.
They keep the COA and one shared raw-material register, so every member's batches trace to the same lot.
Each member saves money every month, and the group builds a record of trust and paperwork that supports later steps such as a shared workshop or joint registration.
Registering the group

Cooperative societies in Nigeria are registered through the cooperative department of the state government. A business name or company is registered with the CAC. Visit your state cooperative office for current requirements before collecting any money from members, and keep written accounts that every member can see.
Bigger batches, bigger risks

At 100 kg, a caustic or LABSA splash involves more chemical and more heat. Keep the same order of addition, add caustic in more portions with longer waits, never lift drums alone, and train every member in PPE and first aid before she works in the room.

The science
Surfactants and pH in plain words
Surfactant: one end loves oil, one loves water
Grease needs alkaline: about 9 to 11
Limescale and urine scale need acid: about 2
Germs need a disinfectant after cleaning
Never put BKC into LAS or SLES products
Oil and water do not mix. A surfactant is a molecule with two ends. One end pushes into the grease, the other stays in the water, and with rubbing the grease floats away in the rinse.
The pH scale runs from 0 to 14, and 7 is neutral. Grease on clothes and floors needs an alkaline cleaner, about pH 9 to 11.
Mineral scale in toilets needs acid, about pH 2.
And germs need a disinfectant, used after cleaning.
One warning. BKC, a disinfectant, has a positive charge. LAS and SLES have a negative charge. Mixed together they cancel each other and form a cloudy, useless mess.

Mixing rules that prevent splashing

Goggles, gloves, apron, long sleeves on

Most injuries happen while weighing concentrates, dissolving caustic soda, or pouring one liquid into another. So splash goggles and gloves go on first. Ordinary glasses do not protect from the side.

LABSA also goes into water, while you stir.
Add the caustic solution to the diluted acid slowly, in portions, because neutralising makes heat.
And label every bucket, even if it is only for an hour.
The rule in every module: bleach with acid releases chlorine gas, and bleach with ammonia releases toxic chloramine gases. Never let them share a container, drain or toilet.

Neutralise first, then the rest

Full PPE on, window open
About 12 kg water, then LABSA in slowly

Goggles, gloves, apron and long sleeves on. Open the window.
Weigh about 12 kg of water into a plastic drum, then pour in the LABSA slowly while stirring with a long paddle.
Dissolve the caustic flakes into cold water in a separate jug, then add it to the drum in portions, waiting between each. The drum gets warm.
After about 90%, test with a pH strip. Keep adding small amounts until the pH is about 7 to 8. If you overshoot, add a very small amount of LABSA, 20 g at a time.
Only now add the soda ash, so it does not fizz. Then CMC, sprinkled slowly, then the SLES, stirred gently.
Rest it overnight so the foam rises, check the pH is about 9 to 10, and fill.

Funke thickens with salt, step by step

Dish liquid touches hands for a long time, so it stops at about pH 7, with no soda ash.

Why this matters
Each product carries its own hazard

Honest claims on every label
These three products each carry a specific hazard. The toilet gel is an acid.

Toilet cleaner
Why citric acid, not hydrochloric
Hydrochloric acid
Easier to handle in a workshop
The ring in a toilet is mostly mineral scale from hard water and urine.
It needs an acid plus time.
Many shop cleaners use hydrochloric acid, spirit of salt.
It is fast, but it gives off corrosive fumes, burns skin badly and eats metal fittings.
This course uses citric acid.
It works more slowly, so a thick gel clings to the bowl, and your directions give it time: leave for at least 10 minutes, or overnight for heavy scale, then brush and flush.
Step by step
Making a 10 kg toilet gel
Label: Do not use with bleach. Dangerous gas can be released.
Goggles and gloves on
About 8.5 kg water in a plastic drum
50 g xanthan gum stirred into 100 g glycerine
Stir in the slurry 10 to 15 minutes
Add 1.00 kg citric acid, then AEO-9
Rest overnight; pH about 2
Goggles and gloves on, because citric acid dust stings the eyes.
In a cup, stir the 50 g of xanthan gum into 100 g of glycerine. This stops lumps.
Pour it in while stirring hard, for 10 to 15 minutes, until it thickens.
Add the citric acid slowly until it dissolves, then the AEO-9. We use this nonionic surfactant because SLES breaks down in acid.
Rest it overnight and record the pH. Every toilet cleaner label must warn: do not use with bleach, because acid plus bleach releases chlorine gas, and toilets are small closed rooms.
Glass and surfaces
A streak-free spray without ammonia
Very little surfactant: 0.3% SLES
Distilled or deionised water only
Isopropyl alcohol added last
No flames, no smoking, window open
No ammonia: no chloramine risk
Streaks come from too much surfactant, minerals in the water, and slow drying. So glass cleaner uses very little SLES.
Use distilled or deionised water. Test it by letting a few drops dry on a mirror. Good water leaves no ring.
Add the isopropyl alcohol last, pouring slowly, and close its container immediately. It makes the spray dry fast.
Its vapour can catch fire from a flame some distance away. Switch off any stove or generator nearby, and keep a fire extinguisher by the door.
We leave out ammonia, so no customer can make toxic gas by later spraying bleach on the same surface.

20 kg x 0.2% = 40 g active BKC
AEO-9 200 g, fragrance 60 g, water 19,660 g
BKC 50% goes in last, slowly
For example, Adaeze in Enugu buys BKC 50%. Her supplier's technical sheet gives 0.2% active BKC for hard surfaces, with a 10-minute contact time. Do not take these figures from social media.
For 20 kg, she needs 40 g of active BKC.
Her concentrate is only 50% BKC, so she needs 80 g of it.
She adds AEO-9 for cleaning power, and fragrance mixed into it first.

What your disinfectant label says
Do print
Leave wet for the contact time
Warning panel and batch number
Do not print
Kills 99.9% of germs, untested
Protects people from disease
Use on skin, wounds or food
Dirt shields germs, so directions start with: clean first. The surface must stay wet for the full contact time. Spraying and wiping dry at once does not work.
And keep BKC away from dish liquid. In a jar test, the mix turns cloudy, and that BKC can no longer kill germs.

Never suggest it protects people from disease.
And speak to your NAFDAC state office before selling anything called a disinfectant.
